title: The Bread of Life
summary: Near Passover, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish, then withdraws when they try to make him king, and comes to his disciples walking on the sea. The next day in the synagogue at Capernaum he tells the crowd that he himself is the bread of life come down from heaven, and that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Many disciples find the teaching too hard and leave, but Peter confesses that Jesus has the words of eternal life.
story: Chapter 5 ended in Jerusalem with the authorities seeking Jesus' life. Chapter 6 moves back to Galilee and to the crowds, and it traces a second kind of rejection. The authorities in Jerusalem rejected Jesus openly; here many of his own followers, who were glad to be fed, turn away when he explains what the sign means. The chapter is a sifting. It moves from a crowd of thousands, to a synagogue audience that grumbles, to disciples who leave, and finally to the Twelve, one of whom will betray him. It is also the first of the great “I am” sayings in John, which will run through the Gospel as a series of pictures of who Jesus is.
historical:
John dates the feeding by the calendar: “the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near” (6:4). Passover, held in spring, remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt, and the whole chapter is shaped by that memory: a crowd in a wild place, bread given from God, a crossing of the sea, and grumbling like Israel's in the wilderness. The Sea of Galilee is also called the Sea of Tiberias (6:1), after the city Herod Antipas founded on its western shore around AD 20 and named for the emperor Tiberius. Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee under Rome throughout Jesus' ministry.

The crowd's attempt to make Jesus king by force (6:15) belongs to a tense time. Judea had been under Roman rule for nearly a century, and popular movements around prophetic or royal figures rose repeatedly in the first century, usually ending in Roman crackdowns. A leader who could feed a crowd in the wilderness looked to some like the long-awaited deliverer. Jesus refuses a crown offered on those terms. The synagogue at Capernaum, where the discourse ends (6:59), was a local meeting place for prayer, the reading of Scripture, and teaching; the remains of a later limestone synagogue there stand on older foundations, which some archaeologists identify as the synagogue of Jesus' day.
cultural:
Barley bread was the food of ordinary and poor people, cheaper than wheat. Philip's figure of two hundred denarii would have been roughly eight months' wages for a laborer, since a denarius was a common day's pay. The feeding also echoes a story from the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42-44). The crowd's response, calling Jesus “the Prophet who is to come into the world” (6:14), reflects the hope based on Deuteronomy 18:15 that God would raise up a prophet like Moses.

The manna was the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16). By the first century some Jewish writings, such as the apocalypse known as 2 Baruch, expected that the treasury of manna would come down again in the age to come. The crowd's challenge, citing “He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (6:31, drawing on Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16), assumes that a greater Moses would repeat the wilderness miracle. Jesus answers that the true bread is not a food but a person. Talk of eating flesh and drinking blood would have been shocking, since the law strictly forbade consuming blood (Leviticus 17:10-14).
literary: The chapter has a sign (6:1-15), a second sign on the sea (6:16-21), and a long dialogue that moves in stages (6:22-71). The dialogue works like a sermon on a text: the crowd quotes a Scripture about bread from heaven, and Jesus takes it apart phrase by phrase. It wasn't Moses who gave but the Father who gives; the bread from heaven is not manna but the one who came down; and eating it means believing, then, more starkly, eating his flesh. The claim “I am the bread of life” comes twice (6:35, 48), with a variation in 6:51. On the sea Jesus says, “It is I; do not be afraid” (6:20), which in Greek is literally I am, the phrase God uses of himself in Exodus 3 and Isaiah. The word grumble ties the crowd to Israel in the wilderness. The chapter narrows as it goes, ending with the few who stay.

outline.t: Jesus feeds the five thousand and refuses to be made king
Jesus walks on the sea: “It is I”
The crowd seeks a sign; Jesus is the bread of life
The grumbling: bread that came down from heaven
Eating his flesh and drinking his blood

doctrines.note: Eternal life comes by believing in the Son, which the chapter pictures as eating: receiving him as life itself, not only agreeing with him. It is also the Father's gift. No one comes “unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (6:44), and none the Father gives will be lost (6:39).

The chapter places God's initiative and human response side by side: the Father gives and draws, and yet people are called to come and believe and are responsible when they turn back. Christians in the Reformed tradition read 6:37-44 as teaching effectual grace; Arminian and other traditions read the drawing as extended to all (compare 12:32). John doesn't resolve the tension for us.

Many Christians hear the Lord's Supper in 6:51-58, though John records no institution of the meal at the Last Supper. How closely the chapter refers to the sacrament is debated; see the hard question.

words.note: Artos, bread or loaf. It appears twenty-one times in the chapter. In the ancient world bread was the basic food, so to say “I am the bread of life” (6:35) is to claim to be what a person cannot live without, not an extra.

Katabainō, to come down or descend. Jesus repeatedly says he has come down from heaven (6:33, 38, 41, 50, 51, 58). The word marks his origin: he is not merely a prophet sent from among the people but one who was with the Father and came. The crowd's objection in 6:42 is precisely that they know his family.

Trōgō, to eat, originally to chew or munch. From 6:54 onward John switches from the ordinary verb for eating to this more physical word. Some interpreters see an emphasis on real, bodily eating that points to the Supper; others think the change is simply a variation in style. Either way it makes the language harder, not easier, to spiritualize away.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble or to offend. “Does this offend you?” (6:61). A skandalon was a trap or an obstacle that trips someone. Jesus' words about his flesh become the point where many disciples stumble and turn back.

christ: The chapter presents Jesus as the fulfillment of the exodus. Moses led Israel through the sea and God fed them with manna; Jesus feeds the multitude in the wilderness, walks on the sea, and then says that he himself is the true bread God sends. The phrase “which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh” (6:51) looks ahead to the cross, where his body is given. His authority reaches past death: four times he promises to raise believers “at the last day.” And Peter's confession, “You are the Holy One of God” (6:69), shows that faith is not a response to a full stomach but to Jesus himself, even when his words are hard.

hard.q: Is Jesus talking about the Lord's Supper when he speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood?
hard.a:
Christians have long disagreed. The Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches generally read 6:51-58 as a direct reference to the Eucharist, in which believers receive Christ's body and blood. Lutherans also see a strong connection with the real presence of Christ in the Supper. Many Reformed interpreters see the Supper in view but stress that Christ is received by faith through the Spirit, pointing to 6:63, “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” Others, including many Baptists and evangelicals, read the passage primarily as a vivid metaphor for believing in Jesus and his death, noting that 6:35 and 6:47 make believing the way to life, and that John's first readers would already know the Supper but that Jesus' hearers at Capernaum could not.

Most readers across these traditions agree on two points. The passage is about receiving the crucified Christ himself as life, not about a ritual performed without faith, and it would be strange for Christians who share the Supper to hear it without thinking of the table. The precise relation of the two is a second-order question on which faithful churches differ.

questions: The crowd wanted Jesus to keep feeding them but left when he offered himself. What do you want from God more than you want God?
Peter stays not because he understands everything but because he has nowhere else to go. When has that kind of faith held you?
What is the difference between believing things about Jesus and feeding on him, as this chapter pictures it?
